nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: Why is understanding heat tolerance in corals critical for restoration projects?
nodes.answer: Understanding heat tolerance is critical for determining the viability of coral populations and for selecting suitable corals to propagate for restoration projects.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Reef degradation induced by climate change is motivating interest in active management strategies to retain living coral cover including coral restoration. Understand- ing the level and range of heat tolerance available in coral populations is critical to determining their viability and may be important in choosing corals to propagate for restoration projects. There is a need to assess heat tolerance experimen- tally and to relate experimental performance to real-world bleaching conditions and outcomes. We sampled a model population of a key reef-building coral (Montipora capitata ) in K ne ohe Bay, O ahu, Hawai i and subjected fragments to an artificial heat stress profile. We subsequently revisited and assessed source colonies at the height of a natural bleach- ing event. Measurements of photosystem efficiency taken on samples during artificial heat stress were predictive of subsequent field bleaching responses of source colonies. By including experimental performance in additive modeling along with previous measures of symbiont community and source site characteristics, we improved predictions of later field outcomes. Survival of coral samples measured several months after experiencing the heat stress had strong positive predictive value for bleaching outcomes but also produced many false negatives.

nodes.question: How does knowledge of heat tolerance benefit coral restoration projects?
nodes.answer: It allows for the selection of coral stocks for propagation based on their heat tolerance relative to others of the same species in the same locale, which is crucial for effective restoration.
nodes.paragraph: Exploring intrapopulation variation in heat stress performance helps explain the full complexity of ther - mal tolerance and has practical applications such as identi- fying high-performing individuals for active management work and predicting population response for planning and setting expectations. For example, choosing coral stocks for propagation in proactive restoration projects requires knowl- edge of the heat tolerance of individuals relative to others of the same species in the same locale (Caruso et al. 2021). Any form of selection risks reducing diversity, which can be counter-productive to conservation aims especially at small effective population sizes (Baums et al. 2019). Understand- ing and detecting the partitioning of heat tolerance across the holobiont will aid in maintaining diversity by expanding the selection pool. There is growing interest in using artificial heat stress to evaluate coral performance because it allows examination of physiological and molecular responses and host symbi- ont interactions in controlled and reproducible conditions (McLachlan et al. 2020). The performance of corals during acute experimental heat treatments (measured by various metrics including visual bleaching scores, fluorometry val- ues, and chlorophyll levels) is commonly used as a proxy for thermal resilience in the wild, but this work primarily focuses on contrasting groups of corals across species, sites, and environmental gradients (van Woesik et al.

nodes.question: How long were the coral fragments acclimated to laboratory conditions?
nodes.answer: The coral fragments were acclimated for 12 weeks.

Collections In early November 2017, one fragment (~ 20 cm3) was col-lected from each of 5 tagged colonies at each study site to represent the patch reef population. Using genotype assign- ments (Caruso and Rocha de Souza et al. 2022), we detected 5 clonal pairs and one triplet and selected one sample of 401 Coral Reefs (2025) 44:399 409 each to yield a set of unique coral genotypes for final analy - sis. To assess genotype effects, we also collected 25 repli- cate fragments from 8 unique M. capitata genotypes from two previously established study sites (Barott et al. 2021). All fragments were glued on labeled aragonite plugs and acclimated to laboratory conditions for 12 weeks in outdoor seawater tables (Fig. 1B). Experimental temperature profiles We distributed fragments haphazardly into 10 indoor flow- through tanks (40 L) in late January 2018. Tank temperature was controlled with Apex aquarium controllers (Neptune Systems), and temperature was recorded on Hobo Pendant loggers (Onset Computer Corp) every 15 min.

nodes.question: At what age can juvenile COTS transition to a coral diet?
nodes.answer: Juvenile COTS can transition to a coral diet as early as four to six months of age.
nodes.paragraph: 2016; Lucas 1984; Neil et al. 2022; Wilmes et al. 2020a; Yamaguchi 1974; Zann et al. 1987). Juvenile COTS can transition to a coral diet as early as four to six months of age and 8 10 mm diameter (Lucas 1984; Yama- guchi 1974). On an algal diet in the absence of coral prey, juveniles reach a maximum size of 16 18 mm diameter fol- lowed by years-long growth stasis (Deaker et al. 2020b). In nature, the size of juvenile COTS at the diet switch to corals is highly variable (Zann et al. 1987; Wilmes et al. 2020a). In situ studies have found large juveniles on CCA (10 32 mm diameter) (Zann et al. 1987; Wilmes et al. 2020a). When the juveniles become coral predators, they grow quickly (Yamaguchi 1973, 1974; Lucas 1984; Zann et al. 1987 ; Birkeland and Lucas 1990 ). The age-size discon - nect of juvenile COTS, where the age of individual juveniles cannot be discerned from their size, presents a challenge to modelling growth.

nodes.question: According to the paragraph, what can expelled symbionts potentially do?
nodes.answer: Expelled symbionts can remain photosynthetically competent and may be reacquired by neighboring adult corals or coral recruits.
nodes.paragraph: 1987; McCloskey et al. 1996; Zhou et al. 2017; Yamashita et al. 2010). Moreover, because expelled symbiont can remain photosynthetically competent after expulsion, they can potentially be reacquired by neighboring adult corals or coral recruits (Ralph et al. 2001; Williamson et al. 2021). However, very little research has explored species-specific variation in ambient expulsion rates or temporal drivers of symbiont regulation (Cui et al. 2023; Yamashita et al. 2010). Research into symbiont expulsion under non-bleaching conditions is vital to better understand symbiont turnover, symbiont community composition, and ambient environmental availability as well as coral-algal symbiosis plasticity and can help us contextualize the effect of thermal stress and bleaching on coral-algal symbiosis. Here we developed a lab-based assay to quantify diel expulsion rates from replicate coral fragments in order to quantify, for the first time, diel patterns of symbiont expulsion under ambient conditions across a variety of Caribbean reef-building coral species. Our results offer insight into the mechanisms driving symbiont turnover and community composition and can inform future work on coral-algal symbiosis during bleaching and subsequent recovery.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Why was it necessary to give the coral fragments time to heal before measuring symbionts?
nodes.answer: It was necessary to prevent the loss of symbionts from tissue lesions caused by the fragmentation process.
nodes.paragraph: Methods Coral collections Thirty-two colonies of the reef-building scleractinians Montastraea cavernosa (Mcav), Pseudodiploria clivosa (Pcli), Orbicella faveolata (Ofav), Siderastrea siderea (Ssid), Diploria labyrinthiformis (Dlab), and Acropora cervicornis (Acer) were opportunistically collected between December 2020 and February 2022 from salvage operations on reefs between Biscayne National Park and the Port of Miami in south Florida, USA (under permit SAL-22-2243C- SCRP). Between four and eight genets of each species (Mcav, n = 5; Pcli, n = 8; Ofav, n = 5; Ssid, n = 5, Dlab, n = 4; Acer, n = 4) were fragmented into 2.5-cm-diameter circular cores using a drill press or 5 cm2 ramets (A. cervicornis) and given ample time to heal (at least 2 weeks). This was done to prevent measuring loss of symbionts from tissue lesions. Two replicate fragments per genet were used throughout the experiment. Symbiont sampling Incubation chambers were pre-prepared with 150 mL of 0.2 m filtered seawater (FSW). This was done to ensure that symbionts observed in the seawater were due to expulsion rather than a product of free-living symbionts in the water source.

nodes.question: How was the fragment tissue surface area calculated?
nodes.answer: The fragment tissue surface area was calculated using ImageJ (v. 1.51) by tracing the circumference or dimensions of the coral fragments in photographs.
nodes.paragraph: The remaining cell pellet was vortexed, removed, and resuspended to a total volume of 1.5 mL using 0.2 m FSW. Lugols solution (10%) was added to preserve the Symbiodiniaceae cells, which were stored at 4 C before being processed on a hemocytometer within two months of collection. Calculating fragment tissue surface area Fragment tissue surface area was calculated in ImageJ (v. 1.51) using photographs collected during sampling. Photographs were uploaded individually to ImageJ and sized so that the entire coral fragment and ruler were visible. The straight segment tool was then utilized to set a scale of a known distance of 1 cm as shown on the ruler in the image (Known Distance = 1, Unit of Length = cm). Once distance was standardized, the polygon selection tool was utilized to trace the circumference of the fragment (massive species) or utilized to trace the diameter and height of the fragment (Acer). The measure tool was then utilized to calculate area for the massive species while the area of the Acer fragments was calculated using the curved surface area of a cylinder (2 rh ) and curved surface area of a cone ( rl ) area calculations to best approximate tissue surface area of the base (cylinder) and tip (cone) of the fragment.
